07-001.r: Energy flow falls at each higher trophic level → second law of thermodynamics: every energy transfer or transformation wastes (dissipates) some energy.

07-002.r: Triple point → the unique temperature and pressure where solid, liquid and gas coexist; triple point of water = 273.16 K (0.01°C).

07-003.r: Radiation transfers heat by electromagnetic waves without any medium, e.g. the Sun's heat across space; conduction and convection need a medium.

07-004.r: Convection (heat transfer by actual movement of matter) happens only in fluids: liquids and gases.

07-005.r: Thermos flask: a vacuum gap between the inner chamber and outer wall stops heat loss or gain by conduction, convection and radiation.

07-006.r: Steam at 100°C burns worse than water at 100°C because it gives more heat: its latent heat of vaporisation (540 calories per gram).

07-009.r: Only 3 true: AC takes heat from room air at evaporator coils, ejects it at condenser. Steam has 540 cal/g more than boiling water; fusion (80 cal/g) ≠ vaporisation (540).

07-010.r: 1 g ice at 0°C → steam at 100°C: 80 (melting) + 100 (heating) + 540 (vaporising) = 720 calories.

07-011.r: °F = (9/5) × °C + 32 (based on water's freezing and boiling points on both scales).

07-012.r: Celsius and Fahrenheit thermometers read the same at −40° (C/5 = (F − 32)/9).
07-012.h: Minus forty is the meeting point of °C and °F.

07-015.r: Fahrenheit reading is double the Celsius reading at 160°C (put F = 2C in C/5 = (F − 32)/9).

07-020.r: Kelvin scale has no negative values: 0 K (−273.15°C) is absolute zero, where particles have no kinetic energy.

07-022.r: Celsius–Fahrenheit relation F = (9/5)C + 32; the same relation holds between the average temperatures in C and F.

07-025.r: Cold countries use alcohol, not mercury, in thermometers because alcohol's freezing point is very low (about −112°C).

07-026.r: Antifreeze in car engines → ethylene glycol; a mix of 60% ethylene glycol and 40% water freezes only at −45°C.

07-027.r: Absolute zero = theoretically the lowest possible temperature: 0 K = −273.15°C, where atoms are completely at rest.

07-028.r: Expansion on heating increases volume, so density (mass/volume) decreases.

07-029.r: Ice (like cast iron, antimony, bismuth, brass) decreases in volume on melting; such solids float in their own melt.

07-030.r: Heating graph: liquid Q (curved line) reached 100°C faster than liquid P (straight line).

07-031.r: Thermostat → automatically regulates and keeps the temperature of a system stable; it helps save energy.

07-036.r: Safest fridge temperature for food → 4°C; cold only slows microbes. Bacteria grow fastest at 40–140°F ('Danger Zone'), so keep the fridge at 35–40°F or below.

07-037.r: Soggy biscuits turn crisp in a fridge because the air inside has low humidity (frost-free fridges remove moisture), so extra moisture is taken out.

07-038.r: Ice cools a drink because it takes latent heat from the drink to melt: A and R true, R explains A.

07-039.r: A true: large cold-storage plants use ammonia, home fridges use chlorofluorocarbons. R false: ammonia liquefies at ambient temperature only under high, not low, pressure.

07-040.r: Ice collecting in a freezer reduces cooling because ice is a poor conductor of heat: A and R true, R explains A.

07-041.r: A glass rod heated in steam expands in both length and width.

07-042.r: A heated metal ring expands, including its inner hole, so the heated ball can still pass through it.

07-043.r: Bimetallic strip: on heating it bends into a curve, with the metal that expands more (A) on the outer side.

07-044.r: Copper feels hotter than glass at the same temperature because copper is a good conductor of heat; R (copper is denser) is true but not the reason.

07-045.r: In winter an iron rod feels colder than a log of wood because iron is a good conductor of heat and wood a poor one.

07-046.r: Warmer air can hold more water vapour: air's capacity to hold moisture rises with temperature.

07-047.r: A true: relative humidity falls as air temperature rises. R true: absolute humidity rises with evaporation. R does not explain A.

07-048.r: Dew does not form on a windy night because strong wind makes evaporation fast.

07-049.r: Not true: 'both maintain humidity'. An AC controls temperature, humidity and air motion; an air cooler controls temperature and air motion, not humidity.

07-051.r: A desert (swamp) cooler works by evaporative cooling.

07-052.r: Cooling, as in air conditioners, is done by releasing compressed gas.

07-053.r: Wet clothes dry fastest at low humidity and high temperature: 20% RH at 60°C.

07-054.r: Adding salt to water raises its boiling point and lowers its freezing point.

07-056.r: At high places low air pressure lowers water's boiling point; salt raises it slightly, aiding cooking. A and R true, but R (low temperature) doesn't explain A.

07-057.r: Thermos bottle walls (glass or steel) are coated with a silver layer to keep drinks at the same temperature.

07-058.r: White clothes are comfortable in summer because they reflect heat; grey or dull clothes absorb heat, so they suit winter.

07-061.r: Light-coloured clothes are preferred in summer because light colours are poor absorbers of heat: A and R true, R explains A.

07-062.r: Water loss by sweating depends on both atmospheric temperature and humidity (and on work rate).

07-063.r: Main function of perspiration → regulating body temperature (sweat cools the body).

07-064.r: A fan gives comfort in hot weather because it makes our sweat evaporate quickly, creating a cooling effect.

07-065.r: Humid heat feels unpleasant because sweat does not evaporate in humid air; evaporating sweat is what cools us.

07-066.r: Evaporation of sweat is an endothermic (physical) process: it absorbs heat from the skin and cools the body.
07-066.t: Not exothermic and not a chemical reaction: only a physical change.

07-067.r: A true: evaporating sweat takes latent heat from the skin and cools the body. R true: high humidity on hot days increases discomfort. R doesn't explain A.

07-068.r: In summer we feel humid heat when the weather is humid.

07-069.r: Xeric condition → low humidity, an inadequate water supply (arid habitats, extremely cold habitats, salt marshes).

07-070.r: Water stays cool in an earthen pitcher due to evaporation: water seeps out through tiny pores and absorbs heat to evaporate.

07-071.r: Cooling rate depends on temperature difference: Churu 95 − 48 = 47°, Shimla 71 − 24 = 47°, so both cups reach room temperature together.

07-072.r: Newton's law of cooling: heat-loss rate ∝ temperature difference with surroundings → cooling 75→60°C takes more than the 25 s for 90→75°C.

07-073.r: Heat wave: maximum temperature at least 40°C in plains and 30°C in hilly regions; the statements swapped them, so neither is correct.

07-074.r: We don't feel the huge atmospheric pressure because our blood exerts a pressure slightly more than that of the atmosphere.

07-075.r: Not true: 'solute raises water potential' (it lowers it). A solution has a higher boiling point and lower vapour pressure than pure water.

07-076.r: At high altitude, lower atmospheric pressure lowers the boiling point, so water boils below 100°C.

07-077.r: A true: boiling point of water falls as altitude rises. R false: atmospheric pressure decreases, not increases, with altitude.

07-078.r: A pressure cooker cooks faster because high pressure raises water's boiling point (to about 120°C).
07-078.h: Pressure up → boiling point up (cooker); pressure down → boiling point down (mountains).

07-084.r: A pressure-cooker handle is ebonite because it is a heat insulator (prevents burns); ebonite is also hard, but that is not the reason.

07-085.r: Cooking temperature in a pressure cooker depends on the area of the lid's hole and the weight on the lid (1 and 3), not on the flame's temperature.

07-087.r: A corked bottle of water breaks in a freezer because water expands (its volume increases) on freezing.

07-089.r: Floating ice melts → water level stays the same: the melt water fills exactly the space the submerged ice took.

07-090.r: Cloudy nights are warmer: clouds act like a blanket, trapping and reflecting back the heat given off by the Earth.

07-091.r: Cloudy nights are warmer than clear ones because clouds prevent radiation of heat from the ground and air and reflect it back.

07-092.r: Neither true: low, thick clouds mainly reflect sunlight and cool the surface; high, thin clouds let sunlight through and trap outgoing infrared.

07-093.r: Statement II true: water's specific heat is higher than land's (water has the highest specific heat). Statement I (land–ocean contrast greater in summer than winter) is false.

07-094.r: Fruits last longer in a cold chamber because low temperature slows their respiration (and ripening).

07-095.r: Woollen clothes keep us warm because air trapped between the fibres is a poor conductor of heat; R (special protein fibre) is false.

07-096.r: Not correct: 'humidity lowers sound speed'. Moist air is less dense, so sound goes faster. Sound speed rises with temperature; pressure, amplitude, frequency don't affect it.

07-097.r: Opening a fridge door in a room warms the room a little: the motor keeps running to cool and adds heat to the room.

08-001.r: Sound waves are mechanical waves (longitudinal in air and fluids); radio waves, X-rays and light are electromagnetic waves.

08-003.r: Sound in air (and any fluid) is a longitudinal wave: particles vibrate parallel to the direction in which the wave moves.

08-004.r: Wavelength = distance between two consecutive compressions (or rarefactions); in transverse waves, between crests or troughs. Speed = wavelength × frequency.

08-005.r: A plucked sitar string sends a transverse wave that reflects at the fixed ends, forming a stationary transverse wave.

08-006.r: The ionosphere (about 50–400 miles up, ionised by solar radiation) reflects long radio waves back to Earth for distant communication.

08-009.r: UHF waves (300 MHz–3 GHz) neither follow the ground nor reflect from the ionosphere; they travel by line of sight, i.e. space waves.
